case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may excuse or extend the 30-day deadline for filing a notice of removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) based on equitable considerations (e.g., equitable tolling).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (the 30-day procedural time limit for removal after receipt of the initial pleading).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that district courts have authority to excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline through equitable doctrines (such as equitable tolling or other equitable exceptions), particularly where strong federal interests are implicated (including interstate/international energy transportation, treaty-related issues, and the need for a federal forum). Petitioners and supporting amici contend that removal timing rules—like many limitations-type periods—are ordinarily presumed to incorporate equitable tolling unless Congress clearly forecloses it, and that the Sixth Circuit wrongly treated the deadline as categorically inflexible.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is a mandatory, congressionally chosen procedural limit on removal that courts lack power to forgive on equitable grounds (or, at minimum, that no equitable exception should apply on these facts). Respondent-aligned amici (federal courts/civil procedure scholars, multi-state amici, Center for Litigation & Courts) emphasize that removal is purely statutory, federalism values counsel against expanding removal beyond what Congress authorized, and allowing equitable exceptions would undermine administrability and invite satellite litigation over timeliness; some amici further argue the Court can affirm without deciding any broad equitable-exception question because petitioners cannot satisfy any such standard here.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains Irwin/Holland’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are typically tollable, but I agree with Justice Barrett that Nutraceutical squarely warns against treating mandatory claim-processing rules as judicially “malleable” absent some textual footing. Justice Thomas’s textual comparison—that Congress expressly authorizes enlargements elsewhere (e.g., § 1441(d)) while § 1446(b)(1) says “shall be filed within 30 days” and § 1446 itself contains carefully drawn alternative triggers and a targeted bad-faith exception—strengthens the inference that courts should not add an equitable overlay by implication. I would therefore rest on narrow, administrable grounds: once a plaintiff timely invokes § 1447(c), the district court must enforce § 1446(b)(1)’s deadline and may not excuse noncompliance except where Congress has specified an exception, preserving uniformity and the federalism-sensitive balance in removal.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are tollable—does not overcome § 1446(b)(1)’s categorical text (“shall be filed within 30 days”) and the statute’s careful internal calibration of timing rules. As Justice Barrett emphasizes via Nutraceutical, mandatory claim-processing rules are not judicially “malleable” absent a textual basis, and § 1446’s express, limited variations (including § 1446(b)(3) and § 1446(c)’s bad-faith exception) rebut any inference that courts may add equitable tolling by silence. Chief Justice Roberts is right that nonjurisdictionality means waiver/forfeiture is possible under § 1447(c), but it does not create a freestanding equitable power to excuse a properly preserved defect. In a purely statutory, federalism-sensitive removal regime, Hallstrom’s separation-of-powers warning applies with full force: we enforce Congress’s deadline as written and leave any further flexibility to Congress.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional statutory deadlines are ordinarily tollable, but § 1446(b)(1)’s categorical “shall be filed within 30 days” and the surrounding, highly specific removal timing scheme rebut that presumption. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Nutraceutical is especially influential: even when a deadline is nonjurisdictional, courts lack authority to create equitable extensions absent some textual hook, and § 1446 already contains the tailored flexibility Congress chose (e.g., § 1446(b)(3) and the express bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)). Justice Thomas’s comparison to statutes that expressly allow enlargement “for cause shown” underscores that Congress knows how to grant tolling-like discretion and did not do so here. Given the federalism-sensitive context and the predictable satellite litigation tolling would invite, I see no legal basis to depart from enforcing the 30-day rule when timely raised under § 1447(c).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains Irwin/Holland’s presumption that nonjurisdictional statutory deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling, especially to avoid harsh results for blameless litigants. But Justice Barrett’s point (echoed by the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan) that Nutraceutical treats mandatory claim-processing deadlines as “unalterable” absent a textual foothold is persuasive here because § 1446 is not a general limitations statute—it is a detailed, calibrated removal scheme with specific alternative triggers and an express bad-faith exception in § 1446(c), which together rebut a free-floating tolling presumption. Even under my pragmatic, access-to-justice lens, equitable tolling in removal would predictably create satellite litigation and delay that often burdens plaintiffs and vulnerable parties seeking timely resolution in their chosen forum, while expanding a defendant’s unilateral power to displace state courts beyond what Congress specified. I therefore remain convinced that when a plaintiff timely moves to remand under § 1447(c), courts must enforce § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day limit as written, leaving any additional equitable safety valve to Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest petitioner point remains Irwin/Holland’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but § 1446’s integrated, trigger-based timing design supplies the “contrary congressional intent” that rebuts that presumption: Congress added specific later-trigger and exception provisions (§ 1446(b)(3), § 1446(c)) and did not leave an open-ended equitable safety valve. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Nutraceutical is especially persuasive for me: even conceding nonjurisdictionality, a properly invoked mandatory claim-processing rule can be unalterable when the statutory scheme is calibrated for administrability and predictability, as removal is. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism/administrability concern underscores why judge-made tolling would be a poor fit here—turning a bright-line removal window into satellite litigation over diligence and prejudice—so enforcing the 30-day command when timely raised under § 1447(c) best respects the statute’s text and structure. Nothing in the Irwin/Holland line overcomes the negative implication created by Congress’s express, limited exceptions in this very section.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are typically amenable to equitable tolling, but that presumption yields where statutory text and structure indicate otherwise. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Nutraceutical is decisive for my methodology: even a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule can be “unalterable” when Congress supplies a detailed, enumerated timing scheme, and § 1446 does exactly that (including targeted alternatives like § 1446(b)(3) and the express bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)). Justice Thomas’s comparison to provisions where Congress expressly authorizes enlargement (e.g., § 1441(d)) reinforces the negative implication and the separation-of-powers concern with grafting equity onto a purely statutory, federalism-sensitive removal mechanism. The nonjurisdictional label means waiver/forfeiture is possible under § 1447(c), not that courts may excuse a timely raised defect by inventing extra-textual tolling.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling, but in this statutory removal setting that presumption is rebutted by Congress’s detailed, bright-line timing scheme. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively tie Nutraceutical to § 1446’s structure: even nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules can be “unalterable” when Congress supplies specific triggers and exceptions (notably § 1446(b)(3) and the express bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)), implying courts should not add a free-floating equitable overlay. Justice Thomas’s comparison to provisions where Congress expressly authorizes enlargement (e.g., § 1441(d)) reinforces, under a text/history/tradition approach, that the absence of similar language in § 1446(b)(1) is meaningful. Because equitable tolling here would invite satellite litigation and unpredictability in a federalism-sensitive, purely statutory mechanism, I would enforce the 30-day rule when a plaintiff timely invokes § 1447(c).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains Irwin/Holland’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but the text and statutory design here rebut it. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1446 supplies a detailed, trigger-based timing scheme and even an express bad-faith carveout in § 1446(c), making it difficult to justify an additional judge-made extension without rewriting Congress’s calibrated framework. Justice Thomas’s comparison to provisions where Congress expressly allows enlargement (e.g., § 1441(d)) strengthens the negative implication that silence in § 1446(b)(1) is meaningful, and Nutraceutical reinforces that mandatory claim-processing rules can be “unalterable” absent textual authorization even if nonjurisdictional. I therefore continue to think courts must enforce the 30-day requirement when a plaintiff timely invokes § 1447(c), leaving any equitable modification to Congress.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest petitioner-side point remains Irwin/Holland’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are generally tollable, but I agree with Justice Barrett that Nutraceutical underscores a critical limit: even nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules can be “unalterable” when the statute’s text and design supply no foothold for equitable exceptions. In this removal setting—where the defendant’s unilateral action displaces the plaintiff’s chosen state forum—the structural federalism concern and the need for administrable, predictable timing rules rebut any background tolling presumption, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize. And Justice Thomas’s textual point about Congress’s targeted timing variations and express exceptions within § 1446 (and its willingness to authorize extensions elsewhere) strengthens the negative inference that courts should not add tolling here. On pragmatic fairness grounds, equitable tolling would also invite satellite litigation over diligence and prejudice that would delay resolution and disproportionately burden plaintiffs who timely seek remand under § 1447(c).

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a mandatory 30-day window for removal, and § 1447(c) instructs remand when a timely motion identifies a procedural defect such as untimeliness—reflecting Congress’s choice to tightly cabin removal and protect federalism interests. Even if the deadline is best classified as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule under the Court’s Arbaugh/Henderson framework, we have been reluctant to create atextual equitable exceptions to filing deadlines where the statutory scheme indicates rigidity and Congress has provided specific, limited exceptions elsewhere (as in § 1446(c)’s express bad-faith exception). Nutraceutical cautions against treating procedural deadlines as “malleable in every respect,” and extending equitable tolling here would invite satellite litigation and undermine the administrable, predictable operation of the removal statutes. On these narrow grounds, I would hold district courts lack authority to excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline absent a congressionally authorized exception.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that the defendant “shall” file a notice of removal within 30 days of the specified triggering event, and nothing in the text authorizes courts to excuse noncompliance on equitable grounds; removal is purely statutory and must be confined to the limits Congress enacted. Congress demonstrated it knows how to create exceptions or confer extension authority when it wishes, as in § 1446(b)(3) and § 1441(d) (permitting enlargement “for cause shown” in foreign-state cases), which counsels against judicially implying equitable tolling here. Murphy Bros. underscores Congress’s aim of uniform, nationally applicable removal timing rules, an aim undermined by case-by-case equitable exceptions. And under Bowles v. Russell, courts lack authority to create equitable exceptions to congressionally prescribed filing deadlines absent textual authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) states in mandatory terms that the notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days” after receipt of the initial pleading, and nothing in the text authorizes courts to extend that deadline on equitable grounds. As this Court has emphasized, courts “are not at liberty to create an exception where Congress has declined to do so,” Hallstrom v. Tillamook, 493 U.S. 20, 27 (1989), and we should be especially reluctant to graft equitable exceptions onto a purely statutory removal scheme that implicates federalism and administrability concerns. Although the 30-day limit is properly treated as a nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule, that does not mean it is judicially expandable; Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), underscores that statutory timing rules are to be enforced as written absent congressional authorization. Allowing equitable tolling here would invite satellite litigation over timeliness and undermine the clear, practical line Congress drew for prompt removal decisions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a bright-line, 30-day procedural limit on a defendant’s unilateral power to remove, and the removal scheme should be strictly construed to respect state-court authority absent clear congressional authorization. Even if the deadline is best classified as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule under the Court’s jurisdictionality framework (Bowles v. Russell; Dolan v. United States), that does not mean federal courts may freely invent equitable exceptions to a carefully calibrated statutory removal timetable. Allowing equitable tolling here would invite satellite litigation, delay, and uncertainty—costs that fall heavily on plaintiffs (often less-resourced) seeking timely adjudication—and Congress did not clearly indicate that removal deadlines are subject to equitable extension. The prudent course is to treat § 1446(b)(1)’s deadline as mandatory and enforceable as written, leaving any expansion of removal flexibility to Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a bright-line, 30-day removal procedure keyed to “receipt … of the initial pleading,” and the statute itself supplies specific, textually grounded timing mechanisms elsewhere in § 1446 (e.g., the later-trigger provisions in § 1446(b)(3)), which suggests Congress chose when removal may be delayed and did not invite additional, judge-made extensions. Under our jurisdiction/claim-processing cases, the deadline is likely nonjurisdictional (see Bowles v. Russell’s clear-statement approach), but nonjurisdictional does not mean courts are free to create equitable exceptions where the statutory scheme’s structure and federalism-sensitive removal context counsel administrable, predictable rules. Because removal is purely statutory and shifts cases from state to federal court, I would read § 1446(b)(1) as a mandatory claim-processing rule that must be enforced when properly invoked, rather than presumptively subject to equitable tolling designed for limitations periods. That interpretation best preserves statutory coherence and workability while respecting Congress’s calibrated removal framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a specific, congressionally chosen 30-day period for filing a notice of removal, and removal being purely statutory, courts should not add extra-textual equitable exceptions absent a clear textual warrant. While § 1446(b)(1) is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule, that does not license courts to disregard it; Bowles v. Russell underscores the limited judicial authority to craft equitable exceptions to statutory deadlines and counsels judicial modesty where Congress has specified a time to act. Federalism and separation-of-powers concerns reinforce enforcing removal limits as written rather than expanding federal jurisdiction through equity. If Congress wishes to authorize tolling or extension, it can say so in the statute; § 1446(b)(1) does not.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a mandatory, short, and administrable 30-day removal deadline, and removal is purely statutory—so courts should be reluctant to create extra-statutory equitable exceptions that expand federal jurisdiction at the expense of state-court authority. Although this Court’s cases distinguish jurisdictional rules from nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules (e.g., Bowles v. Russell), the better reading—consistent with history, federalism, and workability—is that Congress meant the removal clock to be strictly enforced, with § 1447(c) supplying the specified mechanism (timely motion to remand) for policing nonjurisdictional defects like untimeliness. Allowing equitable tolling here would invite satellite litigation over diligence and prejudice, undermining the clarity Congress built into removal procedure and the Court’s institutional interest in predictable, uniform rules. Absent a clear textual basis in § 1446 or an established historical practice of tolling removal deadlines, the equitable-tolling presumption should not be extended to this distinctive removal context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days,” mandatory language that, in context, functions as a nonjurisdictional but “unalterable” claim-processing rule when the plaintiff timely seeks remand under § 1447(c). Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, mandatory claim-processing deadlines are not subject to judicially created equitable exceptions absent a clear textual basis, and the availability of equitable tolling is ultimately a question of statutory intent. The Irwin/Holland presumption is rebuttable, and the removal statute’s structure and federalism-sensitive function—shifting adjudicatory authority from state to federal court—provide “good reason to believe” Congress did not authorize extra-textual equitable extensions. Accordingly, a district court may not excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline on equitable grounds when the defect is properly raised.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a firm 30-day, congressionally specified removal deadline, and removal is a purely statutory mechanism that implicates federalism values by pulling cases from state courts; absent clear textual authorization, federal courts should be reluctant to craft equitable exceptions that expand removal beyond what Congress provided. While nonjurisdictional “claims-processing rules” can sometimes be subject to waiver or forfeiture, Bowles v. Russell underscores that courts lack authority to create equitable exceptions to statutory time limits when Congress has spoken in mandatory terms, and the administrability concerns here (satellite litigation over timeliness) weigh heavily against implying tolling. As a matter of procedural fairness and predictable process, strict enforcement of § 1446(b)(1) treats parties evenhandedly and protects the state forum choice unless Congress expressly allows equitable extension. If Congress wishes to permit equitable tolling for removal, it can do so directly, but the statute as written does not confer that discretion on district courts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may excuse or extend the 30-day deadline for filing a notice of removal after receipt of the initial pleading under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) based on equitable considerations (e.g., equitable tolling or other equitable exceptions).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (the 30-day time limit for removal); with related background implications for removal procedure under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1447.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that district courts do have authority to excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline under equitable principles. Petitioners (and supporting amici) characterize the 30-day limit as a non-jurisdictional, procedural claim-processing rule that—like many filing deadlines—presumptively incorporates equitable doctrines unless Congress clearly forecloses them. They emphasize that this dispute implicates uniquely federal interests (including cross-border/international and interstate energy infrastructure issues and treaty-related questions raised by amici), and that rigid enforcement of the deadline would improperly force federal questions and nationally significant controversies to be decided in state court when equity favors allowing removal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is a mandatory procedural constraint that courts lack authority to forgive once violated, and that the Sixth Circuit correctly treated the deadline as not subject to equitable tolling/exceptions absent clear statutory authorization. Respondent (and supporting amici) stress that removal statutes are to be strictly construed and that allowing judge-made exceptions would undermine predictability, invite satellite litigation over equitable excuses, and dilute Congress’s chosen balance between federal and state judicial responsibilities; even if equitable exceptions could exist in theory, amici supporting respondent contend the facts here do not satisfy any properly demanding equitable standard.
key_precedents: No specific Supreme Court case names are provided in the excerpts supplied; amici and merits briefing refer generally to doctrines distinguishing jurisdictional rules from non-jurisdictional claim-processing rules and to the general presumption (disputed here) that limitations periods may incorporate equitable tolling absent a clear statement to the contrary.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press Holland/Boechler/Harrow’s general presumption that nonjurisdictional filing deadlines are equitably tollable, but that presumption is contextual and can be displaced where the statutory scheme gives “good reason to believe” Congress wanted a firm, administrable rule. Justice Kagan’s Nutraceutical point is decisive for me: nonjurisdictional does not mean courts may craft equitable exceptions, and § 1446(b)(1)’s mandatory “shall … within 30 days,” situated within the tightly reticulated removal/remand architecture and enforced through § 1447(c)’s party-policed remand mechanism, reads like an “unalterable” claim-processing rule when timely invoked. In removal—where federalism and predictable forum selection are central—judge-made tolling would predictably generate satellite litigation over “extraordinary circumstances,” undermining the very timetable Congress appeared to choose. I would therefore hold narrowly, as Justice Jackson suggests, only that when the plaintiff timely raises the defect under § 1447(c), the district court lacks authority to equitably toll § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the modern presumption (Holland, Boechler, Harrow) that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable absent a clear contrary command, but that presumption cannot override the enacted text and structure here. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch explain, Nutraceutical underscores that a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule may still be “unalterable” when Congress has set a firm, party-policed deadline; § 1446(b)(1)’s command that the notice “shall be filed within 30 days,” embedded in a reticulated removal/remand scheme with an express waiver-and-remand mechanism in § 1447(c), supplies the “good reason to believe” (Brockamp) Congress foreclosed extra-textual equitable enlargement. Under a textualist/originalist approach, creating equitable tolling would function as a judicial amendment to Congress’s forum-allocation procedure rather than an interpretation of what Congress enacted. The proper safety valve is waiver/forfeiture under § 1447(c), not a court-fashioned tolling doctrine untethered from statutory language.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—the Holland/Boechler/Harrow presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable—does not carry the day because § 1446(b)(1)’s text (“shall be filed within 30 days”) sits inside a tightly reticulated removal scheme where Congress specified other timing adjustments and policed defects through § 1447(c)’s party-invoked remand mechanism. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Nutraceutical matters here: even when a deadline is nonjurisdictional, it can still be “unalterable” when properly invoked, and nothing in § 1446(b)(1) authorizes courts to extend the removal window. The removal context is not a repose-oriented limitations period but a short, forum-allocation gate where predictability and federalism interests are paramount; importing equitable tolling would invite satellite litigation over “extraordinary circumstances” and effectively revise Congress’s calibrated procedure. Accordingly, I see no textual or structural basis to infer a free-floating equitable tolling power, and I would enforce the 30-day rule as written when the plaintiff timely objects under § 1447(c).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that Nutraceutical shows some nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules can be “unalterable” when properly invoked, especially in a detailed procedural scheme. But Nutraceutical’s logic depended on a rule/statutory context that affirmatively constrained equitable enlargement, whereas § 1446(b)(1) sits alongside § 1447(c)’s party-policed forfeiture mechanism for “any defect other than lack of subject matter jurisdiction,” which structurally signals Congress did not intend courts to be categorically disabled from considering equity in extraordinary circumstances. Justice Alito’s “express extensions imply no others” inference is weakened here because the Court’s modern approach (Holland; Boechler; Harrow) starts from a presumption of tollability for nonjurisdictional deadlines absent an unmistakable contrary command, and this statute’s waiver architecture looks more like a choice to make the deadline enforceable when invoked—not categorically immune to equitable backstops. On my pragmatic view, a narrowly cabined tolling doctrine—reserved for truly extraordinary, non-routine impediments—can preserve predictability in the mine run while preventing the removal scheme from arbitrarily denying a federal forum when compliance is impossible despite diligence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains the Holland/Boechler/Harrow presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable absent a clear contrary command, and her emphasis that § 1447(c) makes procedural defects forfeitable. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, this is not a repose-style limitations period; it is a short, forum-allocation gate embedded in a reticulated, timing-specific removal/remand scheme where predictability and federalism are central, making equitable carveouts notably unworkable. Nutraceutical (as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett underscore) reinforces that nonjurisdictional does not mean judicially extendable: a mandatory “shall … within 30 days” directive, paired with Congress’s chosen safety valve of waiver via § 1447(c), supplies the “good reason to believe” Congress foreclosed extra-textual tolling. Sotomayor’s attempt to distinguish Nutraceutical by source (rule vs. statute) doesn’t move me because the key is statutory context and administrability, and here that context points toward an “unalterable” claim-processing rule when timely invoked.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress Holland, Boechler, and Harrow’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are generally tollable, but that presumption is rebutted where statutory context provides “good reason to believe” Congress chose a firm rule. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain, § 1446(b)(1)’s mandatory “shall … within 30 days,” embedded in a reticulated removal/remand scheme and enforced through the party-invoked mechanism of § 1447(c), looks like Nutraceutical’s unalterable claim-processing rule rather than a tollable limitations period. The fact that Congress supplied specific timing rules elsewhere in the removal statute strengthens the inference that courts lack free-floating equitable authority to add another exception. Under a textualist separation-of-powers approach, importing equitable tolling here would be judicial revision of Congress’s calibrated forum-allocation procedure, not faithful interpretation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—rooted in Holland, Boechler, and Harrow—is the modern presumption that nonjurisdictional filing deadlines are equitably tollable absent a clear contrary signal, and her emphasis on § 1447(c)’s forfeiture mechanism is a serious structural argument. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the removal provisions form a tightly reticulated, federalism-sensitive forum-allocation scheme in which Congress appears to have prioritized prompt, predictable determination, with waiver (via § 1447(c)) serving as the safety valve rather than open-ended equitable extensions. Nutraceutical, which Justice Kagan highlights, matters here not because it involved an appellate rule, but because it clarifies the key principle: a claim-processing rule can be nonjurisdictional yet still “unalterable” when the statutory context supplies good reason to believe Congress foreclosed equitable modification. Given § 1446(b)(1)’s mandatory “shall … within 30 days,” the absence of any textual authorization to extend, and the administrability concerns (satellite litigation over “extraordinary circumstances”) Roberts flags, I remain convinced equitable tolling is unavailable when the plaintiff timely invokes the defect.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor rightly presses the Holland/Boechler/Harrow presumption that nonjurisdictional filing deadlines are ordinarily equitably tollable, but that presumption is rebutted where the statute’s text and structure provide “good reason to believe” Congress foreclosed extra-textual exceptions. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 1446(b)(1)’s categorical “shall be filed within 30 days,” situated within a reticulated removal/remand scheme and enforced through § 1447(c)’s party-policed waiver/remand mechanism, looks like the kind of nonjurisdictional yet unalterable claim-processing rule discussed in Nutraceutical. Unlike the review-access limitations settings in Boechler and Harrow, this deadline is a short, federalism-sensitive forum-allocation gate, and importing equitable tolling would invite satellite litigation and effectively rewrite Congress’s calibrated procedure. Under an originalist, textualist approach, absent any textual authorization to extend the 30-day window, courts lack authority to toll it when the plaintiff timely invokes the defect.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—the modern presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable (Holland, Boechler, Harrow)—does real work in many filing-deadline settings, but here the removal statute’s design supplies the “good reason to believe” (Brockamp) Congress opted for a firm, party-policed window. As Justice Kagan emphasizes via Nutraceutical, nonjurisdictional does not mean courts may add equitable carveouts; § 1446(b)(1)’s mandatory “shall … within 30 days,” coupled with § 1447(c)’s tailored motion-to-remand/waiver mechanism, reads like an unalterable claim-processing rule when timely invoked. Sotomayor’s structural argument that forfeiture under § 1447(c) implies flexibility cuts the other way for me: Congress provided a specific safety valve (waiver through inaction), which is hard to reconcile with an additional, judge-made tolling regime that would generate satellite litigation and unpredictability in forum allocation. Given removal’s federalism-sensitive, rule-bound context, I do not see Holland/Boechler/Harrow as undermining the inference that Congress foreclosed equitable tolling here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Although § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day limit is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule under Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and Kwai Fun Wong, equitable tolling still turns on statutory intent. The removal scheme reflects Congress’s choice of a tight, predictable timetable policed through § 1447(c)’s prompt remand mechanism, and strict construction of removal procedures protects federalism and avoids satellite litigation over equitable excuses. Applying Brockamp’s instruction to look for “good reason to believe” Congress foreclosed extra-textual exceptions, the mandatory “shall be filed within 30 days” language in § 1446(b)(1), read in the context of §§ 1441–1447, indicates no equitable extension authority for district courts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) states that the notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days” after receipt of the initial pleading, and nothing in the text authorizes courts to extend that congressionally prescribed deadline on equitable grounds. This Court has emphasized that when Congress sets filing deadlines by statute, courts are not free to create equitable exceptions absent statutory authorization, because doing so would effectively amend the statute. See Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007) (rejecting judge-made equitable exceptions to a congressionally specified time limit for taking an appeal). Given removal’s intrusion on state-court proceedings and the rule that removal statutes are strictly construed, any equitable tolling or exception to § 1446(b)(1) is for Congress—not the courts—to provide.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that the notice of removal "shall be filed within 30 days" after receipt of the initial pleading, and in the removal context—where Congress has carefully calibrated the state–federal balance—courts should not engraft equitable exceptions absent clear statutory authorization. The structure of the removal scheme reinforces that conclusion: Congress included specific, express timing adjustments and extensions in related provisions, which strongly suggests it did not intend an implied equitable-tolling carveout for § 1446(b)(1) (see Arellano v. McDonough, 598 U.S. 1, 9 (2023)). This Court has repeatedly cautioned that courts are "not at liberty to create an exception where Congress has declined to do so" (Hallstrom v. Tillamook, 493 U.S. 20, 27 (1989)) and that statutory deadlines cannot be judicially altered on equitable grounds when the text and context indicate a firm rule (cf. Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007)). Allowing equitable tolling here would invite satellite litigation over excuses, undermine predictable forum determination, and dilute Congress’s choice to require prompt resolution of removal issues.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline is best read as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, because the statute governs a defendant’s timing obligations rather than the court’s adjudicatory power, with removal jurisdiction conferred elsewhere in §§ 1441–1447. Under this Court’s equitable-tolling framework, nonjurisdictional statutory deadlines are presumptively subject to equitable tolling absent a clear congressional statement to the contrary, and nothing in § 1446(b)(1)’s text clearly forecloses equitable exceptions. See Holland v. Florida and the Court’s more recent applications of the same presumption in Boechler and Harrow, which treat similar deadlines as tollable unless Congress unmistakably bars it. Allowing narrow equitable relief in extraordinary cases promotes fairness and access to justice while still respecting Congress’s procedural design through demanding equitable standards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) directs that a notice of removal “shall” be filed within 30 days, and that kind of specific, mandatory timing command is best read as a nonjurisdictional but mandatory claim-processing rule that is not judicially extendable when properly invoked. Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, even nonjurisdictional deadlines are “unalterable” absent statutory text permitting equitable tolling or extension, and § 1446(b)(1) contains no such authorization (unlike provisions where Congress expressly allows enlargement). That reading also fits the structure of §§ 1441–1447, where Congress calibrates federal-state forum choice through tight, workable procedural gates, and it avoids inviting satellite litigation over equities that would undermine predictable removal practice. Although equitable doctrines sometimes apply to limitations periods, the better textual inference here is that Congress chose a bright-line removal window and left deviations to waiver by the plaintiff rather than equitable exceptions crafted by courts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) says a notice of removal "shall" be filed within 30 days after service or receipt of the initial pleading, and nothing in the text authorizes courts to extend that period on equitable grounds. Even if the deadline is nonjurisdictional, this Court has explained that nonjurisdictional deadlines can still be mandatory claim-processing rules that are "unalterable" when properly invoked, and the removal scheme reinforces that Congress, not courts, sets the balance between state and federal forums. Reading equitable tolling into § 1446(b)(1) would invite judge-made exceptions in an area where Congress has legislated detailed, reticulated procedures and where timing defects are policed through § 1447(c)’s prompt motion practice. The better reading, consistent with separation-of-powers and faithful adherence to the statutory text, is that equitable excuses are unavailable absent a clear congressional statement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a firm, short 30-day deadline that functions as a mandatory claim-processing rule in a context where Congress has carefully calibrated the federal–state balance in removal procedure, and this Court has long instructed that removal statutes are to be strictly construed. Although nonjurisdictional deadlines sometimes carry an equitable-tolling presumption, the Court has also recognized that Congress can make a time limit effectively mandatory when the statutory scheme, specificity, and need for administrable rules point that way, and equitable exceptions risk satellite litigation and unpredictability in removal practice. Consistent with institutional concerns and workability, the better reading is that courts may not create judge-made equitable exceptions to § 1446(b)(1)’s deadline absent clearer congressional authorization, even if the provision is not jurisdictional. That approach aligns with the Court’s insistence on clear lines for procedural deadlines and respects Congress’s design for prompt resolution of the removal/remand question under §§ 1441–1447.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets an unequivocal, exception-free command that a notice of removal "shall be filed within 30 days" after receipt of the initial pleading, and nothing in the text authorizes courts to extend that period on equitable grounds. Even if the 30-day limit is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule under Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and Henderson v. Shinseki, that conclusion does not itself confer authority to craft equitable exceptions where Congress has not provided any, particularly in the removal context where Congress has specified detailed timing and procedure in §§ 1446–1447. Allowing equitable tolling would invite judge-made modifications to a tightly drawn statutory scheme that allocates authority between state and federal courts, and methodological consistency favors enforcing the deadline as written. Where Congress has spoken in mandatory terms governing access to a particular forum, this Court has been reluctant to permit equitable alteration absent clear authorization.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days” of receipt of the initial pleading, and § 1447(c) supplies a separate, tightly drawn mechanism for policing procedural defects through a plaintiff’s timely motion to remand—features that indicate Congress chose a predictable, rule-bound removal timetable. Although the deadline is non-jurisdictional (because it is forfeitable if not raised under § 1447(c)), non-jurisdictional claim-processing rules can still be mandatory and “unalterable” when properly invoked. Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert instructs that the absence of jurisdictional force does not make a deadline equitably malleable, and Brockamp/Lozano frame equitable tolling as a question of statutory intent; here the removal scheme’s text and structure supply “good reason to believe” Congress did not authorize judge-made equitable extensions. Given removal’s state-federal balance and the premium Congress placed on prompt, orderly procedure, I would hold district courts may not excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1) on equitable grounds when the defect is timely raised.
